name: Microblading

lead: Microblading is a semi-permanent tattoo in which a technician draws fine hair-like strokes of pigment into the brow skin. It gives thicker, darker or more even brows, and the fuller look is visible straight after the procedure.

A handheld blade deposits pigment, often iron-oxide based, into the upper dermis. Results are reported to last up to about two years with touch-ups, fading gradually depending on pigment, sun exposure and skin type. The published literature is mostly reviews and case reports of complications.

paras: People book a session with a technician, who maps and draws the brow shape; a touch-up is typically recommended around six weeks later and then every 12 to 18 months. Looksmaxxing forums discuss it as a route to thicker brows alongside options like minoxidil, and members debate how natural it looks on men.

Reported complications include allergic reactions, granulomatous reactions, infection and pigment migration. It fades over time, and removal can require laser treatment. In the US there is no federal standard for ink testing.

angle.text: Men and women get microblading for thicker, darker or more symmetrical brows that last roughly a couple of years. A technician tattoos hair-like strokes into the brow, so the fuller look shows straight away. The literature is mostly case reports of complications.

lead: Microblading is a semi-permanent cosmetic tattooing technique for eyebrows in which a technician uses a handheld tool with fine blades or needles to draw hair-like strokes of pigment into the upper dermis, intended to make brows look fuller, darker or more symmetrical.[1][2] A dermatology review describes it as a form of superficial micropigmentation that deposits pigment as deep as the papillary dermis.[3]

Wikipedia reports that the technique was popular in Singapore by about 2007 and in the US and Canada by the mid-2010s, and results are said to last up to about two years, with touch-ups recommended around six weeks and then every 12 to 18 months.[2] Published literature consists largely of reviews and case reports of complications, including allergic reactions, granulomatous reactions and infections.[4][5][6][7] In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a way to get darker, thicker brows, alongside alternatives such as minoxidil.[8][9]
infobox: About 6 weeks after first session, then every 12-18 months
No federal standard for ink testing

paras: Unlike machine tattooing, each stroke is made by hand. Alternative names include eyebrow embroidery, feathering, microstroking, 3D eyebrows and nanoblading.[2] A procedure typically begins with a consultation, measurement and planning of a symmetrical shape; pigments are commonly iron-oxide based, in dark brown or black shades matched to skin tone.[2] Grokipedia describes sessions of roughly one to two hours including numbing, with a follow-up several weeks later.[1]
Eyebrow tattooing began as a medical technique to reduce the look of brow loss, and its uses include alopecia and thinning from aging or over-plucking.[1][2]

Cosmetic eyebrow tattooing became more common in the US and Asia in the 1980s and 1990s, microblading was popular in Singapore by about 2007 and reached the US and Canada by the mid-2010s.[2] A 2021 review attributes much of its popularity to social media.[3]
Fading depends on pigment quality, UV exposure, skin type, skincare products and medications, and pigment may spread and fade unevenly over time.[2]

Wikipedia says the most common problems are misapplication, pigment migration, color change and sometimes hyperpigmentation, and that serious complications are uncommon; risks include bloodborne pathogen transmission, pigment reactions and granulomas.[2]

Case reports in the dermatology literature describe delayed granulomatous reactions after microblading,[4][10] cutaneous sarcoidosis in microbladed brows,[5] allergic contact dermatitis in a patient with nickel sensitization,[6] koebnerization (disease appearing at the site of skin injury),[11] and preseptal cellulitis.[7] A report on mpox transmission attributed to microblading discusses contaminated equipment as a route.[12] A review of technical and clinical complications of cosmetic tattooing covers the wider category.[13]

A pilot study of four patients with Fitzpatrick skin types III-IV reported successful removal of cosmetic eyebrow tattoos with a picosecond 1064/532 nm laser used with a perfluorodecalin-infused patch.[14]
In the United States microblading is not regulated at the federal level and there is no standard for testing the ink; in Canada it is a personal service regulated by individual provinces.[2]

No controlled trials of microblading's cosmetic benefit were identified. The published human literature is made up of narrative reviews and case reports of complications,[3][4][5][6][7][11] plus a four-patient pilot study of laser removal of cosmetic eyebrow tattoos.[14]
